what: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a one-way stream: the browser opens one HTTP request and the server keeps sending text events down it. The EventSource API reconnects by itself and can resume from the last event id.
like: Like a classroom radio: the teacher keeps broadcasting, you only listen, and if the signal drops your radio retunes and tells the teacher the last thing it heard.
why: Perfect for server-to-client updates such as notifications, progress and AI token streams
Automatic reconnect and resume are built into the browser
Plain HTTP, so it works with normal auth, proxies and load balancers

steps.d: new EventSource(url) sends a GET. The server answers 200 with Content-Type text/event-stream and does not close the response.
Each event is a few lines like id:, event: and data:, ended by a blank line. Lines starting with a colon are comments, handy as keep-alives.
onmessage handles unnamed events; addEventListener handles named ones. Append the data to state and render.
If the connection drops, the browser reconnects and sends the Last-Event-ID header, so the server can replay what was missed.
Turn off response buffering on proxies and send a comment about every 15 s so idle connections are not cut.

numbers.l: SSE connections per browser per domain over HTTP/1.1, shared by all tabs
default simultaneous streams over HTTP/2, which removes the 6-connection problem
how often the spec suggests sending a comment line to keep legacy proxies from dropping the stream
an HTTP 204 No Content response tells EventSource to stop reconnecting

choices.d: SSE is simpler when only the server sends. WebSocket is better when the client also sends a lot or you need binary frames.
EventSource is GET-only and cannot set headers. For POST bodies or Authorization headers, read the response stream with fetch, for example with the fetch-event-source library.
Over HTTP/1.1 only about 6 connections per domain are shared across tabs. Serve SSE over HTTP/2 to avoid starving other requests.
Put an id on every event and have the server replay from Last-Event-ID, otherwise reconnects silently lose data.

instead.why: When the client also sends frequent messages or needs binary data
When updates are rare, or the platform cannot hold long connections

breaks.d: A proxy or CDN waits to fill a buffer before forwarding.
breaks.see: Events arrive in big late bursts
breaks.fix: Disable buffering for the route, send Cache-Control: no-cache and periodic comments

breaks.d: More than 6 streams per domain across tabs block other requests.
breaks.see: Pages hang when many tabs are open
breaks.fix: Use HTTP/2, or share one stream between tabs

breaks.d: A non-200 status or wrong content type closes the connection for good.
breaks.see: Stream silently stops after an auth error
breaks.fix: Detect close in onerror, refresh the token, and create a new EventSource

say: For server-to-client updates like notifications or streamed model output, I use SSE: one long HTTP response with text/event-stream.
EventSource reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID, so I give each event an id and the server can replay the gap.
I run it over HTTP/2 and turn off proxy buffering, and if I need POST or an auth header I read the stream with fetch instead of EventSource.

followups.q: Why can't you send an Authorization header with EventSource?
followups.a: The constructor takes only a URL and withCredentials. Use cookies, or stream with fetch, which allows any method and headers.

followups.q: How do you stop a stream cleanly?
followups.a: Call close() on the client; on the server end the response, or return 204 on reconnect so the browser stops retrying.

followups.q: Why do LLM APIs use SSE?
followups.a: Tokens flow one way from server to client over plain HTTP, and SSE gives incremental delivery with simple framing and reconnect behaviour.

today: SSE is the standard transport for streamed AI responses: for example, the Claude API streams a message as server-sent events such as message_start, content_block_delta and message_stop. Browser apps usually read these with fetch streaming so they can POST and send auth headers.

check.q: Which header does the browser send when EventSource reconnects?
check.why: The browser sends the last id it received so the server can resume.

check.a: HTTP/1.1 allows only about 6 connections per domain, shared by all tabs
check.why: HTTP/2 negotiates around 100 streams by default, so tabs do not starve each other.

check.q: You need to POST a prompt and stream the answer. What now?
check.a: Use fetch and read the response stream
check.why: EventSource is GET-only; fetch streaming gives full control of method and headers.
